newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech cbank ready to up rates to keep crown stable.
newsitem.headline: Czech cbank ready to up rates to keep crown stable.

text.p: The main aim of the Czech National Bank (CNB) remains the stability of the crown, and the central bank is prepared to raise interest rates to keep "the development of a stable currency", a senior CNB official said.

"We prefer a non-inflationary development (of the economy) and from this point of view I can certainly say that we are ready at the CNB to go up with interest rates if necessary to follow the policy of a stable currency," Miroslav Hrncir, a CNB bank board member, told an analyst seminar on Tuesday.
The crown has been hit hard in recent weeks after hitting a record high of +5.51 percent against its dollar/mark basket in February, and was lingering around -2.5 percent on Tuesday.
Ludek Niedermeyer, another CNB board member, told the seminar the central bank is closely following the development of the currency, and could intervene on the market if necessary.
"We are very much following the change in the crown's index...and at some time are ready to step in," he said.
"If we see some technical weakening we would consider intervening, but this is difficult and we know it is not a solution in the long run...One longer-term solution is to put rates up," he added.

When asked if the central bank was considering widening the +/-7.5 band from the basket midpoint within which it fixes the crown, Niedermeyer said: "(To change the band) is an option, but up to now, the policies we have tried to develop correspond to present conditions."

He said that pegging the crown to the ECU instead of the current 65/35 percent mark/dollar would be very "tricky", and that raising the weighting of the mark within the basket was "probably not the best policy choice".

"There is still enough room to manoeuvre (with the current basket) but there also is still a peg, which I think is quite important in the micro-economic sphere...and we would like to maintain this peg," he added.

Central bank officials also told analysts that even with the tight monetary policy and the government's recent fiscal tightening, its forecast of real GDP growth in 1997 of between three and four percent was "possible".

Prime MInister Vaclav Klaus said recently he would consider it a success if the Czech economy grew by 2.7 percent in 1997, about 50 percent lower than originally forecast. Czech real GDP growth in 1996 was 4.4 percent.
After several years of strong demand-led growth, the Czech economy has recently showed signs of severe weakening with industrial output contracting in the first two months of the year.
On April 16, the government announced a series of measures aimed at slowing wage growth while easing a burgeoning trade deficit and spurring economic growth.

Hrncir said the CNB was optimistic the measures would hit their target and that the government aim of cutting 25.5 billion crowns from public expenditures could even give the CNB room to ease its policies.

"A fiscal surplus would enable us to to consider going down with interest rates," he said, adding that the CNB would not move immediately if this happened, but only after it saw a clear and solid trend developing.
Parliament approved a balanced 1997 budget with expenditures and revenues equal at 549.1 billion crowns.
But a slowdown in the economy and poor corporate results have led to lower than planned tax revenues, pushing the balance to a deficit of some 12 billion crowns for the first four months of the year.
